section.title: Paul before Felix
section.sectionRationale: The riot and the plot of the previous chapters give way to the first of Paul's formal hearings before Roman power. A hired orator prosecutes; Paul answers point by point; and the governor, gripped and yet unwilling, leaves him in prison for two years. The gospel is now on trial before the empire, exactly as the risen Christ had promised.
section.thesis: Accused of sedition and sacrilege, Paul calmly answers that the true charge against him is the hope of the resurrection; and when he reasons of righteousness, self-control, and coming judgment, it is the judge who trembles, while a clear conscience keeps the prisoner free.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Tertullus prosecutes Paul before Felix; Paul makes his measured defense; the real issue surfaces as the resurrection of the dead; and Felix, alarmed yet greedy, postpones the verdict and leaves Paul bound.

verses.text: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus, who presented to the governor their case against Paul.
When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation.
In every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, we acknowledge this with all gratitude.
But in order not to delay you any further, I beg your indulgence to hear us briefly.
We have found this man to be a pestilence, stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world. He is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes,
and he even tried to desecrate the temple; so we seized him.
By examining him yourself, you will be able to learn the truth about all our charges against him.”
The Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true.

units.label: Paul makes his defense
units.note: worshiping God according to the Way

verses.text: When the governor motioned for Paul to speak, he began his response: “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense.
You can verify for yourself that no more than twelve days ago I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
Yet my accusers did not find me debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city.
Nor can they prove to you any of their charges against me.

I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the {{hodos|Way}}, which they call a sect. I believe everything that is laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets,
and I have the same hope in God that they themselves cherish, that there will be a {{anastasis|resurrection}} of both the righteous and the wicked.
In this hope, I strive always to maintain a clear {{syneidesis|conscience}} before God and man.

units.label: The real issue: the resurrection
units.note: on trial for the hope of the dead raised

verses.text: After several years, then, I returned to Jerusalem to bring alms to my people and to present offerings.
At the time they found me in the temple, I was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar. But there are some Jews from the province of Asia
who ought to appear before you and bring charges, if they have anything against me.
Otherwise, let these men state for themselves any crime they found in me when I stood before the Sanhedrin,
unless it was this one thing I called out as I stood in their presence: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.’”

units.label: Felix trembles and delays
units.note: righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment

verses.text: Then Felix, who was well informed about the Way, adjourned the hearing and said, “When Lysias the commander comes, I will decide your case.”
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs.
After several days, Felix returned with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
As Paul expounded on {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}}, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and said, “You may go for now. When I find the time, I will call for you.”
At the same time, he was hoping that Paul would offer him a bribe. So he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him.
After two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

hodos.gloss: A road or way. The earliest name for the Christian movement was simply the Way, Acts 9:2, echoing Jesus who called Himself the way, John 14:6. Paul insists this Way is not a novel sect but the true worship of the God of the fathers, the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets.

anastasis.gloss: A rising up, resurrection. Paul stakes his whole defense on the hope of resurrection, the raising of both righteous and wicked. In Acts the resurrection is never an abstract doctrine but rests on the raising of Jesus, the firstfruits, which is why this hope keeps landing Paul in court.

syneidesis.gloss: Conscience, the inner knowing that judges one's own conduct. Paul labors to keep a clear conscience before God and man. It is not a claim of sinless perfection but of integrity: he has hidden nothing and wronged no one, so the accusations cannot stick.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, what is just and right. Paul reasons with Felix about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, pressing the gospel on the conscience of a corrupt and immoral judge. The word that should have humbled Felix instead frightened him, and he sent Paul away.

basic.context: Paul has been rescued from a mob and a murder plot and moved to Caesarea, the seat of Roman government. Now the high priest brings a lawyer, Tertullus, to prosecute him before the governor Felix. The charges are political and religious: Paul is a troublemaker, a ringleader of the Nazarenes, and a temple-defiler. Paul answers each charge and points to the one real issue behind them all.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a courtroom scene with three speeches: the prosecution, the defense, and a private conversation. Notice how Luke sets flattering, unproven accusation against calm, verifiable fact. The turning point is Paul's own admission in verses 14 to 21: the thing they cannot forgive is his hope in the resurrection.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul worships God according to the Way, the hodos, the earliest name for the church. His hope is the anastasis, the resurrection of the dead. He keeps a clear syneidesis, conscience, before God and man. And when he reasons with Felix about dikaiosyne, righteousness, self-control, and judgment, the governor is shaken.
basic.typology: Paul on trial before a Roman governor, innocent yet accused, echoes his Lord, who also stood before a governor on false charges of sedition and temple offense. The servant follows the pattern of the Master, and the false witnesses cannot make their case stand.
basic.christ: The unspoken center of the trial is Jesus. The resurrection Paul defends is grounded in the raising of Christ. The Way he confesses is the way of Christ. And when he speaks with Felix about faith in Christ Jesus, and about righteousness and coming judgment, he is preaching the risen Judge to the man who holds his fate.
basic.god: God governs even a rigged trial. Paul is protected, given freedom, and allowed to keep preaching. The God of the fathers whom Paul worships is the same God who will one day judge Felix and every ruler. His providence keeps His servant safe until the appointed testimony in Rome is given.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 23 sets up the plot and transfer to Caesarea. Luke 23 shows Jesus before Pilate on similar charges. Acts 24:15 rests on 1 Corinthians 15, the resurrection of the dead. Acts 24:25 recalls Jesus' warning that we must give account at the judgment.
basic.oneStory: The risen Christ told Paul he must testify in Rome. This trial is one step on that road: the gospel carried up the ladder of Roman authority, from mob to governor, on its way to Caesar and the ends of the earth. Even Paul's imprisonment serves the advance of the word.

context.literary:
The chapter has the shape of a Roman trial in three movements, and Luke gives each a different tone. The first, verses 1 to 9, is the prosecution: a professional orator, Tertullus, opens with two verses of flattery before he gets to a charge, then makes three accusations in rapid order, that Paul is a plague, a ringleader and a profaner of the temple. The second, verses 10 to 21, is Paul's reply, plain and ordered, which answers each charge in turn and then does something Tertullus never did: it confesses the truth. The third, verses 22 to 27, is not a trial at all but a long, private and mostly sad story of a governor who listens, trembles and puts off a decision for two years.

The contrast of speeches is deliberate. Tertullus piles up praise, most excellent Felix, with a lasting peace and many reforms, while the governor's reputation was far from that. Paul's opening is courteous but restrained, resting on one verifiable fact, that he had been in Jerusalem no more than twelve days. His speech is tightly built: a denial of the charges, a confession of what he really believes, the account of why he had come to Jerusalem, and an appeal to missing witnesses. Roman law expected accusers to be present, and verse 19 quietly notes that the Jews from Asia who had started the trouble are not there.

At the center is the one thing Paul admits, verses 14 to 16: he worships the God of the fathers according to the Way, believes all the Law and the Prophets say, and shares a hope in the resurrection of the righteous and the wicked. The chapter closes on the opposite of that confession. Felix is well informed about the Way, verse 22, frightened by the message in verse 25, and still hoping for a bribe in verse 26. Luke shows a man who knows a great deal and chooses to do nothing.
context.historical:
Antonius Felix governed Judea for about eight years from the early 50s. Roman writers, Tacitus among them, describe a man who ruled with the power of a king and the temper of a slave: he had been a freedman, and his rise owed a great deal to the influence of his brother Pallas at the imperial court. His term was marked by unrest, and Josephus tells of the bandit chiefs and the groups of assassins he put down. Luke's own earlier mention of an Egyptian who led four thousand men into the wilderness in Acts 21:38 comes from the same period. A governor with that record was both nervous about disturbances and open to pressure.

Felix's wife, Drusilla, was a Jewish princess, a daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the Herod who killed James in Acts 12. She had been married before; Felix had taken her from her first husband. That fact makes verse 25 sharper: Paul spoke of righteousness and self-control to a man whose marriage began in what Jewish hearers would have regarded as a scandal. Felix's knowledge of the Way, verse 22, is easy to understand. A governor in Caesarea needed to know what the movement was.

The legal setting is also clear. A Roman governor heard cases in person, with accusers present. The Jewish leaders had hired a barrister, which was normal in the provinces, and the prosecution's argument was a mix of political charge, that Paul was stirring up trouble among Jews across the empire, and religious charge, that he profaned the temple. The first would interest Rome; the second was a matter of Jewish law, and Paul points out that no witnesses had come to prove it.

Paul's reference to alms in verse 17 matters. He had brought a collection from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor in Jerusalem, as Romans 15:25 to 26 and 1 Corinthians 16:1 to 3 record. The charge of causing disorder dissolves when you see that he had come to give. Felix's two-year delay ends when Porcius Festus replaces him, around AD 59 or 60, and Felix leaves Paul in prison to do the Jews a favor.
context.canonical:
Paul's central confession in verses 14 to 15 is a claim about the Old Testament: everything laid down in the Law and written in the Prophets points to a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. The clearest root is Daniel 12:2, where many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt. The same two outcomes are in Jesus' words in John 5:28 to 29, where all who are in the graves will hear His voice and come out. Paul, in other words, is not smuggling in a new doctrine. He is saying that the Way is the continuation of what Israel always hoped.

Verse 25 draws on a triple that runs through the Bible: righteousness, self-control and judgment. Righteousness is the covenant standard in the Law and Prophets, self-control appears among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:23, and the coming judgment stands behind Paul's speech in Athens, where God has set a day on which He will judge the world with justice by the Man He appointed, proved by His resurrection, Acts 17:30 to 31. The Hebrews writer adds the sober line that man is appointed to die once and then to face judgment, Hebrews 9:27, and Paul tells the Corinthians that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:10.

The trial before Felix also falls within a larger Gospel pattern. Jesus was accused before a governor of stirring up the people, Luke 23:2 and 14, and found not guilty, yet delivered over. In John 18:36 to 38 Pilate finds no basis for a charge, and still does not act. Felix is another Pilate: a governor who hears the truth, senses its weight, and decides to stay on the safe side. The phrase 'the Way' is rooted in the journey and covenant language of the Old Testament, and in the Gospel of John Jesus calls Himself the way, John 14:6. The shape of the chapter anticipates Paul's later letters from prison, where his chains become a means of advancing the gospel, Philippians 1:12 to 14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke is writing for readers who needed to know that the new faith was neither a political menace nor a betrayal of Israel. The structure of the chapter makes both points. Paul can answer the charge of sedition with simple facts, a visit of twelve days, no crowds gathered, no speeches in the temple, and he can answer the charge of apostasy by insisting that he believes everything in the Law and the Prophets. In Luke's eyes, the Way is the fulfillment of Israel's hope, not a break from it.

He also wants his readers to see a contrast between Paul and Felix. Paul is free in the strict sense that matters, for he keeps a clear conscience before God and man. Felix has power over him but is not free, for he is held by fear, ambition and greed. The chapter is built so that the prisoner looks more at ease than the judge.

Finally, Luke wants every reader to feel the weight of verse 25. The word Paul speaks to Felix is the word that comes to each reader: repentance, a life under God's rule, and a day of reckoning. The line about a 'more convenient time' is placed at the end of the trial so that the reader cannot easily leave without asking what he is putting off.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes how a governor handled a prisoner and a message. Felix's delay, his hope of a bribe and his willingness to leave an innocent man in chains are recorded as facts of his character, not as policies to follow. Nothing in the passage commands Christians to expect release from prison, or to expect that persuasive speech will bring their opponents around.

What can be taken as a guide is Paul's conduct. He tells the truth about his faith without disguise, 'I do confess to you', while staying calm about the accusations. He keeps his conscience clear, verse 16, and he treats an unfriendly official as someone still worth speaking to about Christ. These match what Peter later asks of every believer: to be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks the reason for the hope that is in them, with gentleness and respect, 1 Peter 3:15.

It is also worth noticing what Paul does not do. He does not offer a bribe, though the chapter makes clear Felix hoped for one. He does not soften the message to Felix and Drusilla, though a milder one might have won him quicker freedom. The passage describes the cost of integrity without instructing us to seek it, and leaves us to see that Paul counted the freedom to speak the truth as worth more than the freedom to leave.

debates.question: Why did Felix keep Paul in prison for two years?

views.label: To do the Jews a favor
views.case: Luke states plainly that Felix, wishing to do the Jews a favor, left Paul in prison, verse 27; a governor who leaves a man in chains to keep a hostile group content has chosen politics over justice. This is how Roman officials often handled difficult provincial elites.

views.label: In hope of a bribe
views.case: Luke also says Felix hoped that Paul would offer him money, verse 26, which fits what was known of Felix's character. The frequent private talks in verse 26 would then be a way of keeping the door open for a payment.

views.label: Fear and indecision before a message he could not dismiss
views.case: Verse 25 says Felix was frightened. A man who knows the Way well and has felt the force of a talk on judgment may delay because he cannot act without admitting something, and he cannot admit anything without changing his life.

debates.bearing: The three motives are not exclusive, and Luke gives the first two himself. Together they make Felix a portrait of a person who hears the truth and stalls. The text warns that delay is itself a choice and that 'a convenient time' may never come.

debates.question: Was Paul right to say the resurrection was the one thing on which he was on trial in verse 21?

views.label: Yes, it was the heart of the dispute
views.case: Paul's gospel is that God raised Jesus, and everything else follows. Every hearing in Acts 22 to 26 returns to the resurrection. His words at the Sanhedrin in Acts 23:6 and Festus's summary in Acts 25:19 show the same center.

views.label: Yes, but it was a legal strategy as well
views.case: By naming the resurrection, Paul shows that the charge is not political but a debate within Judaism, which the Roman governor had no need to settle. Gallio had reached the same view in Corinth in Acts 18:14 to 15.

views.label: No, the issue was larger than that
views.case: Some readers point out that the charges also included the temple and Paul's mission to the Gentiles, and that the resurrection of Jesus does not follow simply from the Pharisees' hope. They say that Paul's statement is partial.

debates.bearing: Paul's wording, 'unless it was this one thing', is a careful appeal to a point his accusers could not deny. It leaves out nothing essential, because the risen Jesus is also the reason for the Gentile mission. The passage shows how a faithful witness can name the center without pretending the edges do not exist.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's Greek gives the chapter several fine points. In verse 5 Tertullus calls Paul a loimos, a plague or pestilence. It is a word for a deadly disease, used in Luke 21:11 of the pestilences that will mark the last days. The charge is meant to make Paul sound like a contagion, something a governor must stamp out. Paul answers by simply describing himself as a worshiper, latreuo, in verse 14, the word used of service to God in the temple and in life, and so he turns the picture of an infection into a picture of devotion.

The prosecutor also calls the Christians a hairesis, a sect. In Acts the word is used of the Sadducees in 5:17 and the Pharisees in 15:5 and 26:5, and the original sense is simply a party or school one chooses. Paul accepts the word's neutral meaning but adds that the Way is no break from the fathers. He places himself under the God of our fathers, patroos theos, and says that he believes everything laid down in the Law and the Prophets. Tertullus also calls the movement the Nazoraioi, the Nazarenes, a word taken from Jesus' hometown, which Matthew 2:23 connects to prophecy. What was a term of mockery here is a name Christians could wear.

Verse 16 says Paul strives to keep a conscience that is aproskopos, without offense or stumbling. The same adjective appears in 1 Corinthians 10:32, where Paul says to give no offense to Jews, Greeks or the church of God. Paul's claim is not that he has never been wrong but that he has lived without giving either God or neighbor a justified grievance. The hope he holds in verse 15 is elpis, a confident expectation rather than a wish, and it rests on the resurrection of both righteous and wicked, as in Daniel 12:2.

The scene with Felix is full of verbs of delay. In verse 22 Felix anebaleto, he adjourned or put off, the case; the verb means to postpone. In verse 25 Felix becomes emphobos, terrified, a word Luke uses for the disciples who thought they saw a ghost, Luke 24:5 and 24:37. The fear is real, but it never turns into repentance. His excuse, when I find the time, translates a phrase about a favorable moment, kairos, which Paul elsewhere uses for the present day of salvation, 2 Corinthians 6:2. Felix wants a more convenient moment, and the Bible's word is now.

The theme of favor returns in verse 27. Felix left Paul bound, wishing charita katathesthai, to lay up or deposit a favor with the Jews. The phrase appears again in 25:9, where Festus uses almost the same words, so the two governors are linked by the same cynical aim. The two years of confinement, dietia, are recalled in Acts 28:30, where Paul's later two years in Rome are described with the same word.

typology.type: The governor who finds no guilt and yields to pressure, Luke 23 and John 18
typology.fulfillment: In verses 1 to 27 Paul stands before a governor who hears accusations of stirring up the people and a profaned temple, charges Jesus faced as well, Luke 23:2 and Matthew 26:61. Pilate found no basis for a charge, John 18:38, and still handed Jesus over, as Felix leaves Paul in chains to please his accusers. The escalation is that Jesus was handed over to die, and the cross accomplished what no verdict could, Acts 2:23. The type falls short because Paul was an innocent servant, not a sacrifice; Christ alone bears sin.

The name 'the Way' for the early church is rooted in the language of journey and obedience in the Old Testament, as in Psalm 119:1 and Isaiah 35:8, where a holy way leads God's people home. Jesus says He is the way, the truth and the life, John 14:6, and so the movement takes its name from the person. The escalation lies in moving from a path of law to a person who is the road itself. It falls short only if the name is treated as a mere label; Acts uses it to say that following Jesus is a whole way of life.

typology.type: The resurrection of the just and the unjust, Daniel 12:2
typology.fulfillment: Paul's hope in verse 15 repeats Daniel's picture of many waking from the dust, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt. The correspondence is promise to fulfillment: Daniel gave the hope, and Christ is the firstfruits who guarantees it, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23. Jesus adds that the dead will hear His voice and come out, John 5:28 to 29, so the judge of all is also the one who raises. The pattern falls short in Daniel only where it lacks a name: he describes the event, while the New Testament shows the person who makes it certain.

Felix trembles when Paul speaks of coming judgment, and the same message was given in Athens, where God has set a day to judge the world through a man He appointed, Acts 17:31. The correspondence is between a ruler who sits in judgment and a King who will judge him. The escalation is that earthly judges, whether Felix or Pilate, will themselves stand before the one they tried, John 5:22 and Revelation 20:11 to 12. The pattern falls short only if it is read as mere threat. The same judge is the one who died for sinners, Romans 5:8.

study.christ:
Jesus is named only once in the chapter, in verse 24, yet he stands behind everything Paul says. Felix and Drusilla send for Paul to hear him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. The subject of that private hearing is a person, not a philosophy. Paul does not offer Felix a set of ideas about life; he offers a Lord to be trusted.

The resurrection of the dead that Paul puts at the center of his defense is the resurrection that Christ has begun. In verse 15 Paul refers to the hope that both the righteous and the wicked will rise. The ground of that hope, as he later writes, is that Christ has been raised as the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23. In Acts 17:31 he says God has given proof of the coming judgment by raising the Man He appointed. That is why the topic of righteousness, self-control and judgment in verse 25 is part of the message of Christ, not a separate moral sermon. The judge is the risen Jesus, and the offer of mercy comes from the same person who will judge.

There is also a contrast with the trial of Jesus that is easy to miss. At His own trial, Jesus said very little, and answered Pilate with a statement about a kingdom not of this world, John 18:36. Paul, by contrast, is allowed to speak at length, and he does it so that the gospel can be heard. The apostle's defense is really an invitation. In both cases the person on trial is the one who offers the judge a chance to listen to the truth, and in both cases the judge declines to act on what he hears.

Finally, the chapter shows what Christ's followers are called to. In Acts 9:15 the Lord said Paul would carry His name before Gentiles and their kings, and here that begins in earnest. Paul's two years in custody are not a pause in that commission but a stage of it. Felix's question, as he sends Paul away, is the question Christ puts to every hearer: what will you do with Me now? Felix's answer, some other time, is the most common one, and also the most dangerous.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the God of the fathers, as Paul names Him in verse 14. He is not a new deity introduced by a new sect. The one Paul worships is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who gave the Law and the Prophets, and who has promised a resurrection. The chapter insists on that continuity: the faith of the Way is the old faith brought to its goal.

God's rule is shown without being announced. A hired lawyer, a powerful governor and a hostile high priest assemble in Caesarea, yet nothing in the chapter happens outside His purpose. Paul is protected, given some freedom and allowed visits from his friends, verse 23, and later he will reach Rome. The two years in Caesarea might look wasted, yet the Lord who told Paul he must testify in Rome, Acts 23:11, has not forgotten. Waiting is part of His plan, not a lapse in it.

The chapter also shows God as judge. Paul speaks to Felix of the coming judgment, and Felix is afraid. That fear is appropriate because the One who will judge sees what a governor cannot, including the motives behind a delay and the money a man hopes for. At the same time the offer of the gospel is real; Felix is given repeated opportunities, and nothing in Luke's account suggests he lacked a chance to repent. The God who judges is also the God who patiently speaks, which Paul will describe elsewhere as His kindness meant to lead to repentance, Romans 2:4.

A third attribute is His faithfulness to a hope. Paul says the resurrection is a hope in God that his accusers also cherish, verse 15. God is the one who makes promises and keeps them across centuries, and the Pharisees' hope is not an empty one. For worship, this means trusting a God who has a long memory, who stands behind His word through delay, and who is not mocked by a governor's evasions. The proper response of the believer is the posture Paul shows: a clear conscience, a steady witness, and trust that the same God who rules the courtroom rules the calendar.

crossReferences.note: The night before the journey to Caesarea, the Lord promised Paul he must testify in Rome. The trial before Felix and the two years that follow are the road to that promise. Reading the two chapters together shows that the delay is not an interruption but part of how God keeps His word.

Jesus is accused before Pilate of misleading the nation and stirring up the people, and Pilate finds no guilt in Him. Paul faces the same kind of charge, sedition and a temple offense, before another governor. The pattern shows the servant walking the road of his Lord, and a governor who sees innocence and still fails to act.

Daniel promises that many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame and contempt. This is the Old Testament root of the hope Paul describes in verse 15, a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked, and it supports his claim that the Way holds to the Law and the Prophets.

Jesus says the hour is coming when all who are in the graves will hear His voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment. It confirms Paul's phrase in verse 15 and shows the risen judge is the Son who speaks the word.

In Athens Paul said that God commands all people to repent because He has set a day to judge the world through a man He appointed, proved by raising Him from the dead. The talk with Felix on judgment in verse 25 is the same message, given in a private setting to a person with power.

All of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, to receive what is due for what we have done. This is the weight behind Paul's words to Felix. A governor sitting on a judgment seat is himself headed for one, which explains why Felix grew afraid.

Paul is on his way to Jerusalem to serve the poor saints with a contribution from Macedonia and Achaia. This explains the alms and offerings of verse 17 and exposes the absurdity of the charge: a man who has come to give money to the poor of his own people is hardly a plague.

Self-control is listed among the fruit of the Spirit, the quality Paul spoke of to Felix in verse 25. It shows that the message to the governor was not a stern moral lecture but a description of the life God gives, which Felix, held by his appetites, could see he lacked.

At Corinth the proconsul Gallio dismissed a charge against Paul as a dispute about words, names and Jewish law. The contrast with Felix is instructive: Gallio refused to be a judge of such matters, while Felix stalled, and both show that Roman officials saw no crime in Paul.

Peter urges believers to sanctify Christ as Lord and always be ready to give a defense for the hope that is in them, with gentleness and respect. Paul's speech before Felix is a model of this: a reasoned account of his hope, given without bitterness to a man who held his life in his hands.

study.oneStory:
The first great questions of the Bible are about judgment and hope. In Genesis 3 God judges a rebellious world and promises a seed who will crush the serpent. Every later story of kings, councils and trials is a chapter in how that promise is carried out. The trial before Felix is one more of these chapters. A representative of the greatest power in the world sits in judgment on a prisoner who carries the answer to the question of how the world will be judged, and neither of them fully realizes it.

Look at the way the two sides handle time. Felix lives by the clock of imperial ambition: his term, his favors, his hope of a bribe and the next governor to arrive. Paul lives by a different calendar, the long promise of the resurrection and a day God has set to judge the world, Acts 17:31. The prisoner is the one who sees the end of the story and the governor is the one who cannot. Scripture says the same of the nations in Psalm 2, where the kings of the earth plot while the One in heaven laughs.

The chapter also shows what happens when the gospel meets power. It meets fear, delay and a hope of profit, and it does not win by force or cleverness. Yet it is not defeated either. The two years in custody become part of the road that carries the message to Rome, and the later letters Paul writes from prison, Philippians 1:12 to 14, show how chains served the advance of the word.

In the end, the chapter points to the day when every ruler is judged. The new heavens and new earth are a place where righteousness is at home, 2 Peter 3:13, and where the questions Felix tried to put off are answered for good. Until then Paul's calm confidence is a sign that the story is moving toward the day of the resurrection, the day of the just and the unjust, and the God who has set that day will keep it.

quiz.q: According to Paul, what is the real reason he is on trial?

options.text: The hope of the resurrection of the dead.
options.note: Paul says plainly that the resurrection of the dead is the issue on which he is judged, verse 21.

options.text: His confession that he worships God according to the Way.
options.note: True and related, Paul does confess the Way, but he names the resurrection as the precise charge behind the hostility.

options.text: That he had actually defiled the temple.
options.note: This was the accusation, but Paul shows it cannot be proven; it is a false charge, not the real reason.

options.text: That he had led an armed revolt against Rome.
options.note: No such thing happened; the sedition charge is baseless and unproven.

quiz.q: How does Tertullus open the prosecution?

options.text: With flattery of Felix, then unproven charges that Paul is a seditious ringleader.
options.note: He praises Felix's rule, then accuses Paul of stirring dissension and defiling the temple, charges he cannot prove.

options.text: With a list of Paul's crimes backed by solid witnesses.
options.note: He does make charges, but Luke's point is that they are unsupported; there are no witnesses who can prove them.

options.text: With a fair and neutral summary of the facts.
options.note: The speech is neither fair nor neutral; it begins with calculated flattery and rhetorical accusation.

options.text: By admitting Paul had done nothing wrong.
options.note: The opposite; Tertullus calls Paul a pestilence and seeks his condemnation.

quiz.q: What happened when Paul reasoned with Felix about righteousness, self-control, and judgment?

options.text: Felix became frightened and sent Paul away for a more convenient time.
options.note: Luke says Felix was alarmed and postponed, verse 25, the tragedy of a man who feels the truth but delays.

options.text: Felix listened because he hoped Paul might offer him a bribe.
options.note: True of his ongoing motive, verse 26, but the immediate response to that sermon was fear and delay.

options.text: Felix repented and was baptized on the spot.
options.note: He was moved but did not repent; he put the decision off, which is the opposite of conversion.

options.text: Felix released Paul at once.
options.note: He did not release him; he left Paul in prison for two years.

quiz.q: Why did Felix leave Paul in prison for two years?

options.text: To do the Jews a favor and in hope of a bribe.
options.note: Luke gives both motives, verses 26 to 27: political cowardice and greed, not any proven guilt.

options.text: Because he wished to please the Jewish leaders.
options.note: This is one of the two stated reasons, but it leaves out his hope for money.

options.text: Because the evidence against Paul was strong.
options.note: The evidence was not strong; Paul was innocent, and the delay was a moral failure, not a legal necessity.

options.text: Because Paul had asked to remain in custody.
options.note: Paul made no such request; the imprisonment served Felix's interests, not Paul's.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by worshiping God according to the Way?

options.text: The Way is the true worship of the God of the fathers, fulfilling the Law and the Prophets.
options.note: Paul insists the Way is not a novel sect but the fulfillment of Israel's own Scriptures and hope.

options.text: The Way is the name the early church used for following Jesus.
options.note: True, this was the church's early self-description, but Paul's point here is its continuity with Israel's faith.

options.text: The Way is a breakaway sect that rejects the Old Testament.
options.note: Paul says the opposite; he believes everything in the Law and the Prophets.

options.text: The Way is a Roman religion approved by the state.
options.note: It was neither Roman nor state-approved; it was the faith of Israel fulfilled in Christ.

questions: Paul could face false accusation with a clear conscience because he had hidden nothing. Where in your life would a clear conscience before God and others bring freedom?
The resurrection hope was the thing Paul would not surrender, even in court. How much does the hope of resurrection actually shape the way you live and speak?
Felix was frightened by talk of righteousness, self-control, and judgment, yet he delayed. Where are you tempted to put off responding to God until a more convenient time that never comes?
Paul preached Christ to the very man who held him prisoner. Who has authority over you right now, and how might God be calling you to bear witness there?
God kept Paul safe and useful through two quiet years in prison. How do you respond when God's plan for you seems stalled or delayed?

translationNotes.note: The BSB omits verse 7, following the earliest and best Greek manuscripts, which move from verse 6 to verse 8. A footnote records that the later Received Text adds material at this point: and we would have judged him according to our law. But Lysias the commander came with great force and took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you. Because the addition is not part of the oldest text, the verse number is left unused. We carry the omission faithfully.

The Way translates the Greek hodos, road or way, the earliest name for the Christian movement, Acts 9:2. Paul uses it to stress that following Jesus is the true continuation of Israel's faith, not a breakaway sect.

Self-control renders a Greek term for mastery of the passions; pointed words to Felix, whose marriage to Drusilla and reputation for corruption made righteousness, self-control, and judgment cut close to home.
